title: Sweden’s great warship Vasa sank about 1,300 metres into its maiden voyage

cover.alt: The preserved 17th-century warship Vasa seen from the bow inside the Vasa Museum in Stockholm, its dark hull rising high above the floor with masts and rigging above.

body: On 10 August 1628 the Vasa, the pride of the Swedish navy with 64 guns and close to 500 sculptures, set off from Stockholm, heeled over in a gust and sank after sailing roughly **1,300 m**. She was top-heavy, with too much weight high in the hull and too little stability to recover, and her lower gunports were open, so water poured into the lower gundeck; about 30 people reportedly died. The cold, brackish Baltic has no shipworm, so the hull survived for 333 years until Anders Franzén located it in 1956 and it was raised in 1961. The Vasa Museum, opened in 1990, has welcomed more than 45 million visitors.

slides.alt: Black-and-white photograph from May 1961 of the raised hull of the Vasa, dark and dripping, being moved into a dry dock in Stockholm.
slides.caption: May 1961: the Vasa, afloat again after 333 years on the seabed, is moved into dry dock at Beckholmen in Stockholm.

slides.question: How far did Vasa sail before she sank?
slides.explanation: About 1,300 m. She heeled in a gust, water flooded in through the open lower gunports, and she went down in the harbour at Stockholm.

slides.heading: Vasa in metres: higher or lower?
slides.note: Dimensions as the museum estimates them; the sparred length includes the bowsprit.
slides.explanation: She was 69 m long overall and rose 52.5 m from keel to mast top, yet drew only 4.8 m of water: a tall ship on a shallow footing.

slides.heading: Why she sank
slides.text: Vasa carried too much weight high up: two gundecks, heavy upper works and hundreds of sculptures. With too little stability to recover from a gust she heeled far over, and the open lower gunports let the sea pour onto the lower gundeck. About 30 people reportedly died; the remains of at least 15 were later found.

slides.heading: Why the wood survived
slides.text: The Baltic around Stockholm is cold and brackish, too fresh for the shipworm Teredo navalis, which quickly destroys wood in warmer, saltier seas. Anders Franzén reasoned that a wreck there would be intact, found it in 1956 with a home-made coring probe, and the final lift ended on 24 April 1961.

slides.question: What saved Vasa’s timbers for 333 years?
slides.explanation: The cold, low-salt Baltic keeps out Teredo navalis, the shipworm that eats wrecks in warmer, saltier seas.

slides.label: visitors to the Vasa since her recovery in 1961, counted to the start of 2025
slides.text: She was ordered with 72 guns, but eight had not been delivered when she sailed with 64.
